A1.justification: Both PDFs describe GestureLSM and provide readable text, equations, figures and tables. The complete documents were compared, including v2's supplementary Appendices A–E; v1 ends after its references.

before.justification: v1 reports original gesture-generation benchmarks, component ablations, qualitative examples and a user study involving 20 participants.

after.justification: v2 retains these original empirical results and adds architectural comparisons, acceleration experiments, attention-order results and training-dynamics analysis.

M1.justification: The core RVQ representation, spatial-then-temporal attention, shortcut learning and beta timestep sampling remain unchanged. v2 additionally evaluates applying ReFlow² to GestureLSM for further acceleration in Table 2e, extending the procedure beyond the original shortcut model.

E1.justification: BEAT-X in v1 becomes BEAT2 in v2, with the same EMAGE source, 60 hours, 25 speakers, 1,762 sequences and split reference. Body and facial gesture generation and the avatar-video application remain. Changed qualitative examples and additional model ablations do not establish new dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: v2 substantially expands evaluated alternatives with flattened spatial-temporal attention, Bi-Mamba, autoregressive and masking generators, and additional ReFlow acceleration variants. SynTalker joins the full metric comparison in Table 1, although it already appeared in v1 Figure 2. Figure 6 replaces TalkShow with CaMN in the qualitative comparison.

E3.justification: v1's model-type discussion states that ReFlow uses the proposed optimized time scheduling; v2 specifies uniform sampling for standard Rectified Flow, despite retaining its reported scores. This is a reported protocol revision, without evidence establishing a rerun. New ReFlow fine-tuning/distillation configurations are also evaluated, while dataset splits, core training settings, eight-step default inference and the user-study design remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds tests of flattened versus separate attention, Bi-Mamba, reversed attention order, autoregressive/masking generation and further ReFlow acceleration. Appendix E and Figure 9 newly examine how BC, FGD and diversity evolve during training. Existing quantization, speech-feature, guidance-scale and beta-skewness ablations are retained, often relocated to the supplement.

E5.justification: Figure 7 retains the identical user-study scores and error bars. Neither version explains those error bars or supplies run/seed counts or significance tests. The new training curves and ablation rows introduce no additional uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Core GestureLSM scores remain unchanged, including FGD 4.088 and 4.247 with facial generation. However, MambaTalk's FGD changes from 5.409 to 5.366, with other metrics revised and inference time supplied. DiffSHEG and ProbTalk timings change from 0.066 to 0.112 and 0.151 to 0.231, respectively. Reported relative GestureLSM training cost changes from 1.2 to 1.06. Numerous new ablation results, training trends and qualitative examples are added; revised ReFlow configurations should not be interpreted as same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: The quantization, attention, flow-matching, shortcut-consistency and beta-distribution mathematics retain their substance despite reformatting and renumbering. Appendix C supplies standard formulas explaining existing evaluation metrics, rather than new mathematical definitions or theoretical results. Neither version provides formal theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: The main claims of coherent body-region interaction, high-quality generation and real-time inference remain. However, v2 changes the introduction's diagnosis of prior methods from unified whole-body features to independently modeled body regions, and foregrounds improving flow matching to outperform diffusion as its third contribution.

C2.justification: v1 already favors BC close to ground truth. Appendix E adds a substantive rationale: high early-training BC accompanies exaggerated beat-following, so decreasing BC can reflect more natural motion. v2 also attributes flattened attention's weaker results to feature-flattening complexity and discusses the quality–speed tradeoff of further ReFlow acceleration.

D1.justification: Appendix C newly explains metric implementation, including pretrained features for FGD, complete-test-set diversity with global translation neutralized, and BC motion-beat detection excluding fingers. The codebook, optimizer, training budgets, architecture sizes and A100 hardware details move essentially unchanged from v1 Section 4.2 to v2 Appendix B. The project-page address is retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds references including ViT, Tango, Contextual Gesture, KinMo and several avatar-related works, while removing Rhythmic Gesticulator. It revises the characterization of prior gesture representations from unified to separately modeled regions. The broader positioning around body-region interaction and efficient sampling remains intact.

P1.justification: The abstract and substantial introduction passages are rewritten, method explanations and contribution wording are revised, and the qualitative discussion is shortened and replaced. Implementation details and several ablation discussions move into a newly organized supplement, while the main ablation section is reorganized into module, architecture, generator and acceleration comparisons.

P2.justification: Figures 2–4 are substantially redrawn, including a reorganized pipeline and FPS annotations. Figure 6 is replaced with larger, colored qualitative examples. The main comparison table becomes a smaller single-column display without the venue column, ablation tables are regrouped across the main text and supplement, and Figure 9 adds training curves. Figure 7's underlying chart remains unchanged.

improvement.justification: The added architecture and generator controls better test the reasons for GestureLSM's design, while training analysis and metric implementation details improve evidential support and evaluation transparency. These are useful, bounded gains. The compressed main comparison table is less readable, and unexplained baseline revisions and persistent per-sentence versus per-frame timing ambiguity limit the overall improvement.
